source.title: Grokking in Linear Estimators -- A Solvable Model that Groks without Understanding
source.authors: N. Levi; A. Beck; Yohai Bar-Sinai

record.file_problem: None noted; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study derives and tests grokking in a different, Gaussian-input linear teacher-student setting, and argues that the apparent transition can arise from the accuracy threshold rather than a change from memorization to understanding. It also analyzes weight decay's effects.
record.gate_note: The study's results are on its own linear teacher-student experiments and analyses. It discusses results from other works, but those cited results are not recorded as rows. Several plotted values are not given numerically in the text and are recorded as figure-only.
record.test_reason: Its own analytic and numerical results show grokking-like delayed generalization on non-algorithmic synthetic data: Gaussian-input linear teacher-student regression scored as threshold classification. This bears on V3. The paper also argues that the accuracy jump is an artifact of the accuracy threshold on a continuously falling loss, a specific restating of what grokking is. That is T5. Its weight-decay results do not test V5's efficient-circuit or critical-dataset account.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is right: grokking arises in linear teacher-student models because generalization loss lags training loss, and the accuracy jump is a threshold artifact rather than a memorization-to-understanding transition. Add three points. Grokking time is set mainly by λ=din/Ntr and is non-monotonic in dout. L2 regularization suppresses grokking when overparameterized. The deeper and nonlinear results are preliminary.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses Gaussian inputs, a linear teacher-student model, MSE loss, and full-batch gradient descent, rather than small algorithmic datasets and the original study's transformer setup. It also analyzes deeper networks and weight decay.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported grokking time depends on λ = din/Ntr, output dimension, weight decay, and the accuracy threshold; the initialization discussion says rescaling changes the effective threshold.

fits_no_version.finding: In this model the accuracy jump is fully determined by a smoothly decaying loss crossing ε/4. Nothing qualitative happens at the threshold, so grokking is called an artifact of the accuracy measure.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Grokking-like accuracy jumps can be a metric artifact: a continuous lag of generalization loss behind training loss, read through a thresholded accuracy.

fits_no_version.finding: Weight decay suppresses grokking in the overparameterized regime, where the timescale is set by 1/γ. In the underparameterized regime it adds an asymptotic loss floor (γ²/[4(1−λ)³]) that blocks perfect generalization below a threshold in ε.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Weight decay's effect on grokking delay depends on the parameterization regime (λ) and does not require a circuit-competition account.

record.problems: The analytic results are stated to apply strictly in the gradient-flow limit and for large sample sizes. Several experimental outcomes are presented only in plots without numerical values or uncertainty estimates. The authors describe the deeper-network evidence as preliminary.

untested.parts: All: no circuits, memorizing components or circuit progress measures.
Images, text and molecules (only synthetic Gaussian data). No empirical initialization-scale or weight-norm sweep, and no lazy-to-rich transition.
All: no LLM pretraining or fine-tuning.
All: no efficient-versus-memorizing circuit comparison, critical dataset size or ungrokking.
All: no adaptive-optimizer or softmax floating-point tests; full-batch GD with MSE loss only.

missing.what: Grokking time as a function of λ=din/Ntr: it diverges quadratically near λ→1 and vanishes as λ→0, so shrinking the training set (raising λ toward 1) lengthens the delay. Verified numerically for several ε.
Phase diagrams of grokking time over (γ, dout, λ), including no-grokking regions.
Training label noise analysis: grokking reaches only finite accuracy, not perfect, for small ε.

record.verdict_notes: The evidence is largely analytic (gradient-flow, large-N limits), with figure-only numerical checks and no uncertainty reported. Delay sizes for r1 and r2 are computed from the paper's Eq. 12 with η0=0.01, not read from the text. The paper is inconsistent on initialization: the introduction says rescaling increases grokking time, while Section 3.1.3 says it leaves results unchanged. Gaussian synthetic data is non-algorithmic but is not among V3's named domains.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not test grokking on small algorithmic datasets or whether shrinking such a dataset increases the delay.
It does not identify or track a generalizing circuit, memorizing components, or circuit progress measures.
The study uses Gaussian teacher-student tasks, not images, text, or molecules. It analyzes initialization rescaling but does not test a lazy-to-rich transition or a weight-norm switch.
No LLM pretraining or fine-tuning on realistic data is studied.
The study does not test whether low norm selects a more efficient generalizing circuit, or a critical dataset size and ungrokking below it.
The study does not compare identifiable algorithms learned across runs.
It does not test adaptive-optimizer instabilities or floating-point limits in the softmax.

rows.subject: linear teacher-student model

rows.measure: Training and generalization accuracy over training time
rows.value: Figure 1 shows the training and generalization accuracy curves; the text says the analytic predictions agree with experiments and that perfect generalization is eventually obtained for λ < 1.
rows.note: The curve values are not tabulated. This is a Gaussian-input linear task, not an algorithmic dataset.
rows.check: At λ=0.1, Eq. 12 gives a delay of only about 40 steps (it vanishes as λ→0). The delay exists but is small, so this is not a full grokking-like delay.

rows.subject: linear teacher-student model
rows.operation_detail: Analytically rescaled the student weights at initialization
rows.measure: Training and generalization loss scaling and resulting grokking time at a fixed accuracy threshold
rows.value: The text says rescaling the student weights by α rescales both losses by (1 + α²)/2, equivalent to changing the threshold; at a fixed accuracy threshold this increases the required saturation level and grokking time.
rows.note: This is an analytical rescaling argument, not a reported empirical sweep of initialization scales or a lazy-to-rich transition.
rows.check: This is an analytic argument, not an empirical sweep. Rescaling the initialization only rescales the losses, which is equivalent to changing ε. Section 3.1.3 says this leaves the results unchanged, while the introduction says it increases grokking time. There is no lazy-to-rich switch.

rows.subject: linear teacher-student model
rows.operation_detail: Analyzed gradient descent with L2 weight decay
rows.measure: Late-time training and generalization losses and grokking time
rows.baseline: γ = 0 has losses that decay to 0 for λ < 1
rows.value: Ltr ≃ γ²/[4(1 − λ)]; Lgen ≃ γ²/[4(1 − λ)³]; Δtgrok ≃ log(1 + √λ)/[2η0(1 − √λ)²]. The text says perfect generalization cannot be obtained below a threshold in ε.
rows.note: The analysis reports weight-decay effects but does not test the proposed efficient-circuit mechanism.
rows.check: Analytic weight-decay result: an asymptotic loss floor and a shorter grokking time. It does not measure V5's efficient-circuit preference, critical dataset size or ungrokking.

rows.subject: linear teacher-student model

rows.note: This is a stated analytical result; the study does not identify a generalizing circuit or test a critical dataset size.
rows.check: Analytic statement that weight decay suppresses grokking in the overparameterized regime. It does not measure V5's efficiency account.
